hook: The leader of Athens in its golden age, who built the Parthenon.

pages.x: Pericles was born to a noble Athenian family around 495 BC. His head was so oddly long that comic poets called him "squill-head", after a pointed sea onion, and sculptors always showed him wearing a helmet. He studied with the philosopher Anaxagoras and was famous for never losing his temper.

From about 461 BC Pericles was the leading man in Athens, elected general fifteen years in a row. He paid citizens for serving on juries, so that poor men could take part too. Athens became the most democratic state the world had seen, though women, slaves and foreigners still had no say.

He used money from Athens's allies to rebuild the temples the Persians had burned. On the Acropolis rose the Parthenon, the temple of Athena, built from 447 BC under the sculptor Phidias, with a statue of the goddess in gold and ivory about 12 metres tall inside.

His partner, Aspasia of Miletus, was one of the most talked-about women in Athens: clever and well educated, said even to have taught Socrates the art of speaking. Enemies attacked Pericles through her, and when she was put on trial he is said to have wept before the jury to save her. She was let off.

In 431 BC, honouring the first dead of a war with Sparta, he gave a speech recorded by the historian Thucydides: "Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a few but of the whole people." It remains one of the most famous speeches ever made in praise of a free society.

To fight Sparta, Pericles brought the farmers of Attica inside the walls of Athens. In the crowded city a plague broke out and killed perhaps a quarter of the people, among them his two sons, and in 429 BC Pericles himself.
Pericles led Athens at the height of its golden age, when it gave the world democracy, drama, philosophy and the Parthenon. "The Age of Pericles" still means a city at its creative best.
pts: Led Athenian democracy for over 30 years
Built the Parthenon on the Acropolis
Gave the Funeral Oration in praise of democracy
